facts.claim: DNS names form a tree held in parts by many name servers; a resolver that knows nothing better starts at the root’s servers and follows each referral closer to the name (RFC 1034).
Every DNS answer carries a TTL: the time in seconds it may be cached before it should be thrown away (RFC 1035).
TCP opens a connection with a three-way handshake, SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, and hands data to the application only once the connection is established (RFC 9293).
Before it has measured a round trip, a TCP sender waits 1 second for an acknowledgement, and it rounds any shorter computed timeout up to 1 second, then resends (RFC 6298).
A full TLS 1.3 handshake lets the client send its request after one round trip (RFC 9001 on TLS 1.3).
With a key from an earlier session, a TLS 1.3 client can send early data, 0-RTT, in its very first message (RFC 8446).
Early data can be replayed by an attacker, so clients must only send early data that is safe to repeat; RFC 8446’s examples of harm are buying an item or moving money.
A TLS 1.3 session ticket may last at most 604,800 seconds, 7 days (RFC 8446).
A certificate binds a public key to a name, and a trusted certification authority vouches for that binding by signing it (RFC 5280).
For https, the browser checks that the certificate matches the name it asked for, to stop anyone impersonating that server (RFC 9110).
GET is a safe method, essentially read-only; POST is not on HTTP’s lists of safe or idempotent methods (RFC 9110).
HTTP/1.1 asks clients to limit how many connections they open to one server, and deliberately sets no maximum (RFC 9112).
One HTTP/2 connection carries many requests at once, each on its own stream, their pieces interleaved (RFC 9113).
Over TCP, a lost packet stalls every active HTTP/2 request, whether or not it was the one hit; HTTP/3 over QUIC recovers losses stream by stream (RFC 9114).
QUIC combines the transport and TLS handshakes into one, to cut the time a connection takes to set up (RFC 9000).
The .example name and the address ranges this module uses are reserved for documentation (RFC 2606, RFC 5737).
